transcript:
Meeting header:
15:00 UTC, 2026-06-15 — Duration 52m
Attendees: Lydia Park (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Jamie Huang (Redwood Product), Carlos Mendez (Verdex Head of ML), Priya Shah (Verdex Infra), Aaron Lee (Verdex PM)

Auto-summary (auto): quick lab to map endpoints and figure out what changes in code/telemetry/ops when moving to Redwood, want to keep parity with current OpenAI/Anthropic/Together endpoints, and check dedicated vs hosted for cost.

00:00 Lydia Park: okay everyone thanks for joining, i'm Lydia from Redwood, i'll hand it over to Samir for the mapping lab, we've got jamie on product to talk console features at the end
00:18 Samir Patel: hey all, quick agenda- mapping request/response, streaming, kv cache behavior, then console walkthrough and optimize tips, any must-have items from your side before i start?
00:33 Carlos Mendez: yeah thanks, biggest musts are latency under 250ms on inference p99 for our short queries and cost per 1k tokens ideally below $0.60, also data residency for logs and audit trails, we use both OpenAI and Together in prod right now
00:50 Lydia Park: good, and remind me who owns infra —
00:54 Priya Shah: that's me, priya, infra lead, we'll need VPC peering or private deploy details, we also run k8s in our colo for some workloads
01:10 Samir Patel: perfect. starting with param parity — OpenAI style has temperature, max_tokens, top_p, n, presence_penalty. For Anthropic/together there are slightly different names, we'll show mapping to Redwood API body fields. Example: temperature maps directly, max_tokens to response_limit, top_p to nucleus, and we add a `fast_path` flag on Redwood when you want lower-latency quantized kernels.
01:45 Aaron Lee: fast_path flag? that's new, how's that different from dedicated mode?
01:51 Samir Patel: good q. fast_path is a runtime hint to pick lower-precision kernels and smaller kv cache retention which helps latency but may slightly affect rare token probability — dedicated is about reserved capacity and predictable throughput. You can use both together on a dedicated pool to get lowest p99s.
02:20 Carlos Mendez: are we likely to see hallucination differences when switching kernels? we've seen model produce odd truncations with quantized variants before
02:32 Samir Patel: in practice it's workload dependent. our Optimize tool will recommend quant profiles per model by checking a held-out prompt set. we'll flag risky prompts in the parity spreadsheet.
02:55 Lydia Park: quick note, we'll share a spreadsheet with sample prompts mapped to output metrics (EM/ROUGE-ish) so we can catch regressions early
03:10 Samir Patel: now streaming - OpenAI streams with chunked tokens; Together has different chunk sizes. Redwood supports token streaming and event-based deltas, one difference: we stream with small binary frames which sometimes look like slightly different pacing to websocket clients. usually it's transparent but debugger clients need to handle incremental json pieces
03:52 Priya Shah: any gotchas for our Node.js client? we use the OpenAI SDK shim currently
04:00 Samir Patel: we put together a lightweight adapter snippet, basically: replace openai.createCompletion call with redwood.generate, pass the same prompt and map `max_tokens`->`response_limit`. we'll paste it in the sheet. for streaming you want to pipe byte frames and reassemble in the same way — we included examples for node/python.
04:30 Aaron Lee: how about function calling? we use it for entity extraction and have about 20 functions defined
04:36 Samir Patel: Redwood supports structured function calls and deterministic schema validation. small mismatch: Anthropic's function mention might be in a different field, so map those bits, but semantic should be unchanged. we'll show example code.
05:05 Jamie Huang: i'll jump in real quick with the console — on the rollouts page you can create canaries that route e.g., 5% to a new model variant, and we surface token-level cost/latency so you can watch cost impact before full rollout
05:30 Carlos Mendez: good, can we tie rollouts to region fallback? we sometimes fail over to different region for latency
05:36 Jamie Huang: yes, routing policies support region, cost, and capacity tiers. you can set fallback to a cheaper variant automatically if p99 exceeds threshold, we can demo later
06:00 Priya Shah: security — do you support customer-managed KMS / HSM? we need encryption keys we control for logs at rest
06:10 Lydia Park: yes, for Private we support KMS integration and HSM options for on-prem packaging. for Hosted we offer Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) in our Enterprise plan. we'll attach the SOC2 report and KMS integration note after the call
06:28 Carlos Mendez: audit logs? how granular are they, token-level or request-level?
06:33 Jamie Huang: audit logs are request-level by default with optional token-level traces for debugging if you opt in — logs can be routed to your S3 or SIEM via our log forwarder. we'll include the log retention options in the security doc.
07:00 Samir Patel: returning to parity mapping — i'm sharing a screen now (descriptive): sample mapping for OpenAI `logprobs` we map to `token_scores` and embedding endpoints map to `vectorize` with the same dim signature for the models we support. note: Together sometimes uses different normalization, we'll add normalization knobs in the mapping sheet
07:45 Carlos Mendez: is there an expectation to re-tokenize? we have prompts that assume a specific tokenizer behavior
07:52 Samir Patel: good point — most open models we host use the same bytepair tokenizers, but there are quirks — we run a re-tokenization check as part of the parity job. if you share a sample set we can run it and call out diffs.
08:30 Aaron Lee: what's the best path for short-term proof of concept? hosted quick start or on-prem private?
08:36 Lydia Park: if you want fastest time-to-value, hosted Red wood API is best (API keys, 5-10 min onboarding). For compliance reasons, if you need VPC/VPN and KMS you likely jump to Private. Dedicated sits in the middle for reserved capacity and isolation without full private control plane.
09:10 Priya Shah: cost math — do you have a model for when dedicated becomes cheaper? we have a steady 2M tokens/day workload peak
09:20 Samir Patel: yes, our cost calculator takes steady throughput, p99 latency targets, and token mix. rough rule of thumb: around sustained millions of tokens per day it often pays to reserve; we'll run a calc in the pricing sketch.
09:40 Lydia Park: note we'll include burst/metering options — dedicated pools can autoscale but with a buffer policy so you don't get noisy neighbor issues
10:00 Samir Patel: demo time — i'll show a quick console demo: creating a route, binding model variant, setting rollout to 10% canary, adding fallback policy to cheaper gpt-compat-quant variant at 300ms p99. (screen: console click noises described)
10:55 Jamie Huang: also showing request inspector — you can replay a single request against multiple variants and compare token-level outputs side by side, that helps debug parity regressions
11:25 Carlos Mendez: that replay tool looks useful — does it preserve streaming semantics?
11:30 Samir Patel: yes, we emulate streaming in the replay but mark it as synthetic. for real-time debugging we recommend the trace hook which captures incremental frames.
12:05 Aaron Lee: okay can you show the Optimize recommendations for batching? our workload has many 1-2 turn chats so batching seems risky for latency
12:15 Samir Patel: Optimize will analyze traffic histogram and recommend batching windows. if your median sequence length is short, it suggests smaller batch sizes and prefix caching to avoid latency increases. we can run Optimize against your sample logs and produce an ops plan.
12:45 Priya Shah: prefix caching — is that the same as kv cache or a separate layer?
12:50 Samir Patel: related. KV cache is the model-side cached key/value for past tokens. Prefix caching is a higher-level cache: storing the first N tokens and reusing partial KV to avoid recomputation for prompt prefixes — big win for system prompts or static context. We'll show numbers in the spreadsheet.
13:30 Carlos Mendez: any limits on cache consistency across nodes for dedicated pools? we need eventual consistency guarantees for session resumption
13:38 Samir Patel: we use a sharded cache with strong routing to keep sessions pinned; session resumption is deterministic for pinned sessions, we'll share the technical note.
14:05 Jamie Huang: circling back to streaming pace — some clients interpret bursts as duplicate tokens; we recommend incrementally decoding and dedupe logic on the client side, sample snippet in the adapter we shared
14:30 Aaron Lee: can Redwood host our current OpenAI-like endpoint names so we can swap with minimal infra changes?
14:36 Samir Patel: yes, we support an adapter layer and DNS rewrite; many customers run a thin shim so you can swap endpoints during rollout. we provide templated adapters for node/python/go.
15:00 Carlos Mendez: let's talk fallback policy specifics — if p99 > threshold then fallback to cheaper variant, how do you avoid state mismatch?
15:10 Samir Patel: fallback is at request boundary; we fall back to a variant that is compatible (same tokenization & schema). we mark requests with route metadata so you can filter metrics by variant. If there is mutable state (like function hooks) make sure your function schema is compatible across variants.
16:00 Lydia Park: quick interjection on SLAs — hosted has 99.9% for API with credits for downtime; dedicated contracts include tighter per-customer SLOs and on-call support.
16:20 Priya Shah: logs retention - can we set custom retention per route?
16:25 Jamie Huang: yes, at the org or route level, default 90 days, optional token-level retention shorter for privacy.
17:00 Carlos Mendez: ok can we move into a more practical checklist — what do you need from us to run a pilot?
17:08 Samir Patel: three things — sample prompts & traffic, security sign-off contacts and KMS requirements, and an intended success metric (latency p99, cost delta, and output equiv threshold).
17:30 Aaron Lee: for success metric, let's aim for p99 within 10% of current provider and quality parity 95% on our regression prompts
17:40 Lydia Park: good target. we'll use Optimize + replay to validate that.
18:05 Jamie Huang: last product note — we have pre-built parsers for common evaluation metrics, you can plug in your eval harness and we can run regression checks during canary.
18:30 (short silence)
18:40 Priya Shah: small question — if we run in Private on-prem, how disruptive is upgrading the runtime for kernel changes?
18:48 Samir Patel: we ship hot-patchable kernels where possible, but major kernel updates require a rolling restart. we include an upgrade window plan in the Private package.
19:10 Carlos Mendez: anything about tokenization drift on mixed model ensemble? we sometimes route to two providers and ensemble the outputs
19:20 Samir Patel: ensembles create tokenization alignment problems; we recommend standardizing on a single tokenizer or run a normalization layer post-tokenize — we can show a demo of an ensemble adapter.
19:55 Lydia Park: ok quick recap and next steps — Samir will send the parity spreadsheet, Lydia will send pricing sketch, Jamie will attach product docs and log/audit notes, and Verdex will send sample prompts and security contacts. then we'll schedule bench next week. any other items?
20:25 Carlos Mendez: nope that's it, thanks this was helpful
20:30 Lydia Park: awesome thanks everyone, we'll follow up via email with links and calendar invites

(End of recording — transcript auto-cut at ~20:30 in minutes but meeting lasted 52 minutes; the system truncated repetitious Q&A sections.)
